catalog_quote: Word stress is generally on the penultimate syllable of multisyllabic roots. However, if the penultimate vowel is a mid front lax vowel /E/ and the final vowel is other than /E/, the stress falls on the ultimate syllable. Word stress is not affected by affixation. (Whisler 1992) ... [ST1 notes carried with the passage:] Heavy_for_Stress: non /E/ ... There are five known words that do not conform to this rule, probably explainable historically. (Whisler 1992) ... The (rare) possessive enclitic /mam/, probably borrowed from the local Malay, causes a stress shift. ... A paragogic vowel /E/ is added to clause- and pause-final consonants and semivowels. ... This does not cause a stress shift.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: the StressTyp2-carried Whisler 1992 passage is confirmed verbatim on pp. 7-8 of the source via held Google Books snippets (digest at, together with Whisler's own stress-marked examples ([ˈyeget], [ˈloben], [boˈbane], [salaˈnipe] penult; [mɛˈlit], [feˈfo], [deˈlut], [museˈla], [keˈet] final), fn.1/p.23 on the -mam shift, p.25 on the non-shifting paragoge, and p.31 n.5 restating the /ɛ/-avoidance rule. (2) The deciding source is a 1992 SIL phonology chapter, and per Glottolog 5.1 plus a CrossRef search nothing fuller or instrumental exists; the 1995 CAD intro and Kamholz 2014/2024 are restatements.
